You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Change the background into a basketball court
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Is there visible evidence that the background has begun changing toward a basketball court, even though completion is not established by this check?
node.criteria: Pass if the image shows discernible progress toward replacing the background with a basketball court, including basketball-related scene changes or partial court cues. Fail if there is no visible progress toward that requested background change. Unknown if progress cannot be distinguished from the original or assessed reliably. This is a progress judgment, not a completion judgment; a complete court background may also pass.
node.binding: Assess only progress toward the requested background replacement. Do not use this check to decide whether the background is complete; unrelated edits do not count as progress.

node_traces.evidence: The kitchen background has been replaced with a basketball scene, including a hoop, basketballs, and court markings, showing clear progress toward the requested background change.

fulfillment: The node’s criteria appear to over-require visible court markings: the edited image shows the kitchen replaced by a coherent basketball-court scene, with a hoop, basketballs, and a visible court boundary/marking on the playing surface. Yet s1 treats the plain-looking floor as decisive failure, while s2 recognizes the court markings and progress; the parent consequently returns partial despite the reference yes. Refine the binding and completion criterion to assess the background as a whole and weigh contextual evidence together, rather than making a particular floor appearance or markings an implicit mandatory feature when other visible court cues establish the setting. Keep the distinction between a recognizable court and basketball equipment alone, and do not let s2’s progress signal substitute for completion. The traces are valid and queried, with no transport or dependency failure; this is a semantic evidence/criterion disagreement, not a reason to force the reference label.

The downstream failure is therefore a semantic criterion/evidence aggregation issue in s1 or the parent’s completion judgment, not a defect in s2’s progress decision. Preserve the distinction between progress and completion, and investigate why the whole-scene court evidence was discounted.
